cells.tense: You are at the door with the pen, learning the arrival by hand now.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Take one finished thing — a call, a chore, a favor — and treat it as closed this week, without picking it back up.
cells.core:
Something is entering at a door, and you are apprenticing to it. The arrival is not announced; it is in the flat pack, the new schedule, the person who asked for help and waits. You read the grain by handling what is already here, and the door stays open while you do it. Learning what grows is mostly this: patient attention to what actually sits on the table.

At that door, something is finished and being kept alive by attention. A call returned twice, a chore that has its ending but no rest, a favor that was complete the day it was done. Let that one close. Closing it does not shut the door; it is what makes the next arrival legible. The unfinished work stays yours to carry.
cells.sheetLine: You learn what's arriving by tending what's already here.
cells.verb: apprenticing to how what arrives takes shape
cells.place: the doorway where what is entering is still deciding

cells.tense: You will be bracing at a door that will not open until it is read.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Spend ten minutes feeling toward something you don't yet know about what's coming — no list, no answer, no fixing.
cells.core:
At the door, the arrival is being scripted. You have the next shape mostly built — what it will need, when it will arrive, how it will go — and the reading has run past the door opening. That is care working too hard. It is also how a thing that wanted to arrive at its own pace gets met with a plan instead of a welcome.

The wonder your hands still know is the corrective. Before you name what is next, feel toward it without a shape. Ten minutes, no list, no fixing. What is coming can be sensed before it is solved, and the sensing is not a delay; it is the practice you are already in. Let the picture stay unfinished long enough to be true.
cells.sheetLine: You're building the next arrival before it gets to arrive.
cells.verb: apprenticing to how what arrives takes shape
cells.place: the doorway where what is entering is still deciding

cells.tense: You stood at the door so long it closed on a room already behind you.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin a page, a walk, or a call just because starting it feels alive — and stop before it's done.
cells.core:
At the door, there is no hand reaching for the next thing; the learning has gone quiet. You know how to keep what is already here, but not how to meet what is not yet. What is entering now arrives at a threshold where you are not standing, and the door does not need pushing — it needs a hand on it, yours, curious rather than expert.

The spark you remember is the way back. Begin something because beginning interests you — a page, a walk, a call to someone about nothing. Do not finish it. The point is not the result but the feeling of starting at all; that is how a starved place gets energy, not by effort pushed into it. Start a thing you have no destination for. The door is still there.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to keep, but not how to begin.

cells.tense: The pen is down, and the room around you is already being written.
cells.act: drop one condition you set and take the step
cells.ask: Notice a condition you quietly set before moving — the right moment, the right mood — and take one step without it this week.
cells.core:
You are apprenticing to what is entering, and you are not giving yourself the credit. The door is being read, the shape is being learned by hand, and from the inside it looks like circumstance. A condition — the right moment, the right mood, the right person to check with — has been written into the plan, and it is the part that is most yours. Keeping the step conditional keeps it safe.

Give the step one small test without its condition. Move before the condition is met — a message sent, a thing begun, a question asked — once this week, one step only. Nothing big. When the step works without the condition, your hand in it becomes visible, and you may find the care has been yours steadily, whether or not you were watching it.
cells.sheetLine: The step is already yours, waiting only on a condition.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is already apprenticing to what is entering; the draw only shows the capacity, not that it has been taken up. A reader could reasonably say the open door is still unsure, not that they are busy reading it; the asks survive that objection because they are things anyone can do in a door that is open. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about learning the grain of an arrival before naming it — it admires my own method, so I have cut it.
